title: Bureaucrat SLAMS the Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO)
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman relays and reflects on a moment where a senior Australian education department official, speaking candidly in a forum he declines to name, voiced a criticism of AERO (the Australian Education Research Organisation) that he says many teachers have made privately for years: that AERO's guidance materials, while individually well-researched, have become so voluminous and procedurally hedged that classroom teachers often cannot locate a clear instructional recommendation inside them. Ashman situates this as a specific failure within AERO's own founding mission, which was created precisely to close the research-to-practice gap between evidence sitting in journals and usable Monday-morning lesson plans. He argues the failure mode is that guidance can be faithful to the evidence while being so heavily hedged against every edge case that a teacher reading it late at night cannot extract a clear answer to a simple practical question. Ashman notes he has made this critique of hedged guidance documents before, but argues hearing it voiced from inside the system, from someone whose job depends on the documents working, lands differently and suggests the translation problem is genuinely difficult even for a well-funded organization built specifically to solve it.
points: Relays a candid, unnamed-forum admission from a senior Australian education department official that AERO's guidance has become so hedged that teachers often cannot extract a clear recommendation from it.
Situates the criticism as a failure within AERO's own founding mission, which was created specifically to close the research-to-practice gap between journal evidence and usable classroom guidance.

Identifies the specific failure mode as guidance that is faithful to the evidence yet so heavily qualified against every edge case that it fails the practical test of answering a teacher's simple, concrete question.

Notes that hearing the critique voiced from inside the system, by someone whose job depends on the guidance working, lands differently than the same critique from an outside commentator, and suggests the translation problem is genuinely hard rather than a failure of will.
quotes: AERO's guidance materials, while individually well-researched, have become so voluminous and so procedurally hedged that classroom teachers often cannot actually locate a clear instructional recommendation inside them.

The organization exists because Australian education, for years, suffered from a research-to-practice gap, good evidence sitting in journals that teachers never read or could not easily translate into Monday morning lesson plans.

Guidance that is faithful to the evidence but so heavily qualified, so carefully hedged against every possible edge case and context variation, that a working teacher reading it at nine at night cannot extract a clear answer.
Hedging is not neutral, it has a cost, and the cost falls specifically on the practitioner who needed a usable answer and instead got several pages of caveats.
But hearing it from inside the system, from someone whose job depends on these documents functioning, lands differently than hearing it from outside critics like me.
It's that the translation layer between good research and usable classroom guidance is genuinely difficult to build well, even for an organization explicitly founded to build it.
